summary.text: Vandermonde’s identity gives \(j!\binom{x+k}{j}\equiv j!\binom{x}{j}\pmod{k}\): every term involving a positive part from \(k\) is divisible by \(k\), since \(\binom{k}{r}r!=k(k-1)\cdots(k-r+1)\) and \(r!\mid j!\). Applying this congruence to both binomial factors yields termwise agreement modulo \(k\); after summing to the larger bound, the extra terms vanish because \(\binom{n}{j}=0\) for \(j>n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=n!\,[x^n]\frac{e^x}{(1-x)^n}\qquad(n\ge 0).
\]
We prove that for every pair of nonnegative integers \(n,k\),
\[
a(n+k)\equiv a(n)\pmod{k}.
\]

First we put the sequence into the finite-sum form that will be used in the congruence argument. For \(n\ge 1\), the standard power-series expansions are
\[
e^x=\sum_{r\ge 0}\frac{x^r}{r!},
\qquad
(1-x)^{-n}=\sum_{j\ge 0}\binom{n+j-1}{j}x^j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
[x^n]e^x(1-x)^{-n}
 =\sum_{j=0}^n \binom{n+j-1}{j}\frac1{(n-j)!}.
\]
Multiplying by \(n!\), and using
\[
\frac{n!}{(n-j)!}=\binom nj j!,
\]
gives
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^n \binom nj\binom{n+j-1}{j}j!.
\tag{1}
\]
For \(n=0\), the original coefficient definition gives \(a(0)=[x^0]e^x=1\). Formula (1) remains valid if its sole summand at \(n=j=0\) is interpreted as \(1\). Equivalently, define
\[
T_m(j)=\binom mj\binom{\operatorname{pred}(m+j)}j j!,
\]
where \(\operatorname{pred}(u)=\max(u-1,0)\). Then the formula valid uniformly for every \(m\ge 0\) is
\[
a(m)=\sum_{j=0}^m T_m(j).
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, except at \(m=j=0\), the second binomial coefficient is the ordinary \(\binom{m+j-1}{j}\), while at that exceptional point both binomial coefficients and \(0!\) equal \(1\).

We next prove the elementary congruence that drives the argument.

**Lemma.** For all nonnegative integers \(x,k,j\),
\[
\binom{x+k}{j}j!\equiv \binom{x}{j}j!\pmod{k}.
\tag{3}
\]

By Vandermonde's identity,
\[
\binom{x+k}{j}
 =\sum_{r+s=j}\binom xr\binom ks.
\]
After multiplication by \(j!\), the term with \(s=0\) is exactly
\( inom xj j!\). We show that every term with \(s>0\) is divisible by \(k\).

For such an \(s\), the identity
\[
\binom ks s!=k(k-1)\cdots(k-s+1)
\tag{4}
\]
shows that \(k\mid \binom ks s!\): if \(s\le k\), the product on the right begins with the factor \(k\), and if \(s>k\), then \(\binom ks=0\), so divisibility is again immediate. Since \(s\le j\), we also have \(s!\mid j!\). Hence
\[
k\mid \binom ks j!,
\]
and therefore
\[
k\mid \binom xr\binom ks j!.
\]
Thus all terms of the Vandermonde sum other than the \(s=0\) term vanish modulo \(k\), proving (3). This reasoning also covers \(k=0\): all terms with \(s>0\) then equal zero, and (3) is simply an equality.

We now compare the summands for the arguments \(n+k\) and \(n\). We claim that for every \(j\ge 0\),
\[
T_{n+k}(j)\equiv T_n(j)\pmod{k}.
\tag{5}
\]

If \(j=0\), both sides are equal to \(1\), so the assertion is immediate. Suppose henceforth that \(j>0\). Because \(j\) is positive, there is no truncation issue in taking predecessors, and
\[
\operatorname{pred}(n+k+j)
 =n+k+j-1
 =(n+j-1)+k
 =\operatorname{pred}(n+j)+k.
\tag{6}
\]
For brevity, write
\[
A=\binom{n+k}{j},\quad A_0=\binom nj,
\]
and
\[
B=\binom{\operatorname{pred}(n+k+j)}j,
\quad
B_0=\binom{\operatorname{pred}(n+j)}j.
\]
Applying the lemma first with \(x=\operatorname{pred}(n+j)\), using (6), yields
\[
Bj!\equiv B_0j!\pmod{k}.
\tag{7}
\]
Applying it a second time with \(x=n\) yields
\[
Aj!\equiv A_0j!\pmod{k}.
\tag{8}
\]
We may multiply congruences by arbitrary integers. Therefore (7), followed by a rearrangement of factors, then (8), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{n+k}(j)
 &=ABj!\\
 &=A(Bj!)\\
 &\equiv A(B_0j!)\pmod{k}\\
 &=(Aj!)B_0\\
 &\equiv (A_0j!)B_0\pmod{k}\\
 &=A_0B_0j!\\
 &=T_n(j).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (5), including the separate case \(j=0\).

Using the sum formula (2) for \(a(n+k)\) and adding the termwise congruences (5) over \(0\le j\le n+k\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+k)
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{n+k}T_{n+k}(j)\\
 &\equiv \sum_{j=0}^{n+k}T_n(j)\pmod{k}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]
It remains only to identify the sum on the right. If \(j>n\), then \(\binom nj=0\), and hence \(T_n(j)=0\). Thus extending the upper limit in the sum for \(a(n)\) from \(n\) to \(n+k\) adds only zero terms:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{n+k}T_n(j)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n}T_n(j)
 =a(n).
\tag{10}
\]
Combining (9) and (10) proves
\[
\boxed{a(n+k)\equiv a(n)\pmod{k}}
\]
for all nonnegative integers \(n\) and \(k\), as required.
